name: Identifies formal and informal language
description: Student can listen to or read two short examples of language used in different contexts (e.g. greeting a friend vs. a teacher) and explain which is more formal and why.
exampleOfSuccess: Student listens to 'Hey what's up' and 'Good morning Miss Chen' and correctly explains the second is more formal because it uses a title and full greeting.
commonError: Student identifies one as formal but cannot explain why, focusing only on tone rather than word choice or structure.

name: Matches language to relationship
description: Student can select or write appropriate language for a given relationship (e.g. writing a message to a friend versus a note to a teacher) using vocabulary and tone suited to each.
exampleOfSuccess: Given the prompt 'You need to ask someone to help you find your bag', student writes a casual request to a friend and a polite request to a teacher using different vocabulary.
commonError: Student uses the same phrasing for both, not adjusting for the relationship.

name: Explains why language changes in different roles
description: Student can describe how and why language choices shift depending on the role a person takes on (e.g. student vs. captain of a team vs. speaker at an assembly).
exampleOfSuccess: Student explains: 'When you're the captain you have to tell people what to do, so you use bossy words, but when you're just in the team you ask instead.'
commonError: Student describes what someone says in a role but not why the language changes.

name: Uses culturally respectful language in context
description: Student can explain why certain greetings or expressions of respect are used in specific cultural contexts
sequenceOrder: including First Nations Australian protocols such as Acknowledgement of Country.
exampleOfSuccess: middle
commonError: When asked why we say 'We acknowledge the Traditional Owners of this land', student explains it shows respect for the people whose land we are on and that this is an important cultural protocol.
checkpointTask: Student recites the acknowledgement but cannot explain its purpose or why specific language is used.

name: Adapts own language to context in speaking
description: Student can deliberately adjust their spoken language for two different contexts in a class activity
sequenceOrder: demonstrating awareness of formality through word choice
commonError: late
checkpointTask: During a role-play activity, student uses casual vocabulary and informal structure when talking to a peer, then switches to more formal phrasing and complete sentences when addressing the class.
isOptional: Student changes volume or speed but not vocabulary or sentence structure.

name: Uses 'because' to give a reason for a preference
description: Student can express a preference about a text and follow it with a reason using 'because' or a similar connector.
exampleOfSuccess: Student says or writes: 'I liked this book because the pictures showed what the characters were feeling.'
commonError: Student states a preference without providing a reason, or uses 'because' but the reason is circular ('I liked it because it was good').

name: Uses precise vocabulary to appreciate a text
description: Student can use more specific language than 'good' or 'nice' to describe what they appreciated about a text
sequenceOrder: drawing on vocabulary related to characters
exampleOfSuccess: language or structure.
isOptional: Student says: 'I liked how the author used really short sentences when the wolf was coming — it made it feel scary and fast.'
isArchived: Student uses evaluative language ('I liked it', 'it was interesting') without specifics about what created that effect.

name: Uses preference verbs with different degrees
description: Student can use verbs such as 'liked'
sequenceOrder: 'preferred'
exampleOfSuccess: 'loved' and 'didn't enjoy' to express varying degrees of preference about different texts.
isOptional: When comparing two books, student says: 'I enjoyed both but I preferred the information book because I already liked the topic.'
isArchived: Student uses only 'liked' or 'didn't like' without exploring the range of verbs available.

name: Provides text evidence to support an opinion
description: Student can refer to a specific part of a text (a character's action
sequenceOrder: a sentence
difficultyStage: an image) to support their opinion about it.
commonError: middle
checkpointTask: Student says: 'I think the author wanted us to feel sorry for the character. On page 7 it says she sat alone and looked at the floor — that shows she was sad and left out.'
isOptional: Student gives opinions about texts without referring to specific evidence from the text itself.

name: Writes a structured appreciation of a text
description: Student can write two or more sentences that state a preference
sequenceOrder: give a reason supported by text evidence
difficultyStage: and use specific vocabulary rather than general evaluative language.
commonError: late
checkpointTask: Student writes: 'I preferred the narrative to the information report because the author described the setting in a way that made me imagine being there. The line about the fog creeping over the hill made it feel real and mysterious.'
isOptional: Student writes a preference statement but does not connect it to specific language choices or evidence from the text.

name: Identifies the purpose of a familiar text type
description: Student can name the purpose of a familiar text type (narrative
sequenceOrder: recount
exampleOfSuccess: information report) when shown an example.
isOptional: Student looks at a recipe and says: 'This is a procedure. It tells you how to make something step by step.'
isArchived: Student identifies the topic of the text rather than its purpose ('This is about cooking' instead of 'This tells you how to do something').

name: Names a structural feature of a text type
description: Student can identify and name at least one structural feature of a familiar text type (e.g. orientation in a narrative
sequenceOrder: steps in a procedure
commonError: early
checkpointTask: Student points to the numbered steps in a procedure and says: 'These are the steps. They're in order so you know what to do first.'
isOptional: Student describes what a feature looks like without naming it or explaining its function.

name: Identifies a language feature of a text type
description: Student can identify and explain at least one language feature typical of a given text type (e.g. time connectives in recounts
sequenceOrder: command verbs in procedures
commonError: middle
checkpointTask: Looking at a recount, student identifies: 'It uses words like first, then and after that to show what happened in order — recounts go in time order.'
isOptional: Student identifies a language feature but links it to the wrong text type, or confuses a structural and a language feature.

name: Identifies pronouns used to refer to a person or thing
description: Student can locate personal pronouns (he
sequenceOrder: she
exampleOfSuccess: it
commonError: I) and possessive pronouns (his
ownerTier: my) in a text and identify what they refer back to.
reviewNotes: In the sentence 'Mia picked up the puppy. She held it gently.', student correctly identifies that 'she' refers to Mia and 'it' refers to the puppy.
column16: Student identifies the pronouns but cannot say what they refer to, or links them to the wrong noun.

name: Tracks how a person or thing is referred to across a text
description: Student can follow how the same person or thing is referred to using different words across several sentences (proper noun → pronoun → descriptive noun).
exampleOfSuccess: Given a short passage about 'Lily the rabbit', student maps: 'Lily' → 'she' → 'the rabbit' → 'her' and explains they all mean the same character.
commonError: Student tracks the first reference but loses track when a pronoun or descriptive noun replaces the name.

name: Identifies inferred words in a text
description: Student can locate a point in a text where words have been omitted and identify what has been left out based on context.
exampleOfSuccess: After reading 'Jake ran to school. He arrived late [at school].' student explains: 'It doesn't say 'at school' the second time but we know from the sentence before.'
commonError: Student says words are missing but cannot identify what they are or where the meaning comes from.

name: Uses pronouns to link ideas when writing
description: Student can use personal and possessive pronouns correctly in their own writing to avoid repetition and create cohesion across sentences.
exampleOfSuccess: Instead of writing 'Sam went to the park. Sam played on the swings. Sam had fun.', student writes: 'Sam went to the park. He played on the swings and had a great time.'
commonError: Student overuses the proper noun, repeating it in every sentence rather than substituting pronouns.

name: Explains how pronouns create cohesion
description: Student can explain in their own words why writers use pronouns and omit repeated words
sequenceOrder: linking this to the concept of cohesion (making a text hang together).
exampleOfSuccess: late
commonError: Student explains: 'If you kept saying the character's name every time it would sound boring and choppy. Using 'she' and 'her' makes it flow and sounds more like a real story.'
checkpointTask: Student explains the mechanical substitution but not the effect on the reader or the cohesion of the text.

name: Locates information using a table of contents
description: Student can use a table of contents to find which page a specific chapter or section begins on.
exampleOfSuccess: Given a non-fiction book, student uses the table of contents to find which page the chapter 'Life cycle of a butterfly' starts on and opens to the correct page.
commonError: Student flicks through the book to find the information rather than using the table of contents.

name: Uses an index to locate specific information
description: Student can use an alphabetical index to find where a specific topic or word is discussed in a book.
exampleOfSuccess: Student uses the index to find the page number for 'migration' and turns to the correct page.
commonError: Student looks at the beginning of the index rather than using alphabetical order to locate the entry.

name: Navigates a website using menus and links
description: Student can use a sidebar menu
sequenceOrder: drop-down menu or hyperlink to navigate to a specific section of a website or digital text.
exampleOfSuccess: middle
commonError: Student uses the navigation menu on a class-approved website to move from the homepage to the 'Animals' section and then to 'Rainforest Animals'.
checkpointTask: Student clicks randomly or scrolls the entire page rather than using the navigation tools.

name: Explains the purpose of a navigation feature
description: Student can explain why a specific navigation feature (table of contents
sequenceOrder: index
exampleOfSuccess: link) is useful and when a reader would use it.
isOptional: Student explains: 'You'd use the index if you already know what you're looking for and just need to find the page fast. The table of contents is better if you want to see all the chapters and choose what to read.'
isArchived: Student describes what the feature looks like but not when or why a reader would choose to use it.

name: Identifies a compound sentence
description: Student can identify a compound sentence in a text and name the coordinating conjunction that joins the two clauses.
exampleOfSuccess: Student reads 'The wolf huffed and he puffed and he blew the house down' and correctly identifies 'and' as the conjunction joining the clauses.
commonError: Student identifies the conjunction but labels the whole sentence as two separate sentences.

name: Identifies the two ideas in a compound sentence
description: Student can split a compound sentence into its two independent clauses and explain that each could stand alone as a sentence.
exampleOfSuccess: Student separates 'She was tired but she kept reading' into 'She was tired.' and 'She kept reading.' and confirms both make sense on their own.
commonError: Student cannot identify where one clause ends and the next begins, or identifies the conjunction as part of one of the clauses.

name: Uses 'and'
description: 'but' and 'so' to join ideas
sequenceOrder: Student can construct a compound sentence using each of the three main coordinating conjunctions (and
exampleOfSuccess: so) and explain what relationship each one creates between the clauses.
isOptional: Student writes three sentences: 'It was raining and we stayed inside.', 'I wanted to go but it was too late.', 'She was cold so she got a jumper.' and explains that 'but' shows a contrast and 'so' shows a result.
isArchived: Student uses 'and' for all three, or uses 'so' and 'but' but cannot explain the different relationships they signal.

name: Uses compound sentences in own writing
description: Student can use compound sentences correctly and purposefully in their own writing
sequenceOrder: choosing conjunctions appropriate to the meaning they want to create.
exampleOfSuccess: late
commonError: In a written recount, student writes: 'We walked to the oval and the grass was wet so we had to be careful. I tried to kick the ball but it went the wrong way.'
checkpointTask: Student uses compound sentences but always uses 'and', making the writing feel repetitive and flat.

name: Identifies nouns in a sentence
description: Student can locate the nouns (people
sequenceOrder: places
exampleOfSuccess: ideas) in a simple sentence.
isOptional: In the sentence 'The old dog sat on the warm mat.', student correctly identifies 'dog' and 'mat' as the nouns.
isArchived: Student identifies adjectives ('old', 'warm') as nouns because they also describe things.

name: Identifies the article and adjective extending a noun
description: Student can identify the article (the
sequenceOrder: a
difficultyStage: an) and any adjectives that extend a noun to form a noun group.
commonError: early
checkpointTask: In 'the longest side', student identifies 'the' as the article and 'longest' as the adjective extending the noun 'side'.
isOptional: Student identifies the noun but misses the article or labels the adjective as part of the noun.

name: Builds an extended noun group
description: Student can expand a simple noun into a noun group by adding an article and one or more adjectives that answer questions like 'what kind?' or 'how many?'.
exampleOfSuccess: Starting with 'shoes', student builds: 'two pairs of old walking shoes' by adding 'two pairs of' (how many), 'old' (what kind) and 'walking' (what type).
commonError: Student adds one adjective but does not explore how multiple describing words can stack before a noun.

name: Identifies a verb group in a sentence
description: Student can locate the verb group in a sentence
sequenceOrder: including multi-word verb groups such as 'was touched' or 'had been running'.
exampleOfSuccess: middle
commonError: In 'The door was closed quietly.', student identifies 'was closed' as the verb group and explains it includes two words that together describe the action.
checkpointTask: Student identifies only the main verb and misses auxiliary verbs ('was', 'had', 'is being').

name: Uses noun groups and verb groups in writing
description: Student can deliberately use extended noun groups and multi-word verb groups in their own sentences to add detail and precision.
exampleOfSuccess: Student revises 'The cat sat.' into 'The small striped cat had been sitting on the old wooden fence for hours.' demonstrating awareness of both noun group and verb group expansion.
commonError: Student adds adjectives but leaves verb groups unexpanded, or expands verb groups without attending to noun groups.

name: Identifies what an image adds to a text
description: Student can describe what specific information or meaning an image provides that is not stated in the written words of the text.
exampleOfSuccess: Looking at a diagram of a food chain in a book, student explains: 'The writing talks about what animals eat, but the diagram shows the arrows connecting them so you can see the order.'
commonError: Student describes what the image shows without explaining what it adds beyond the written text.

name: Identifies what an image shows about a character
description: Student can analyse an illustration in a narrative to identify what it reveals about a character's emotions
sequenceOrder: actions or relationships not stated explicitly in the text.
exampleOfSuccess: early
commonError: Student says: 'The words just say the girl sat down, but the picture shows her looking away with her arms crossed — that tells us she was upset or annoyed.'
checkpointTask: Student describes the image literally without drawing inferences about what it communicates about the character.

name: Explains how an image multiplies meaning
description: Student can explain how an image works together with or extends beyond the written text to create a richer or more complex meaning.
exampleOfSuccess: Student explains: 'The text says the town was quiet, but the picture shows broken windows and empty streets — so the image multiplies the meaning by making it feel like something bad happened there.'
commonError: Student says the image 'matches' the text rather than explaining how it adds layers or creates a richer meaning.

name: Selects or creates an image that adds meaning to their own writing
description: Student can choose or describe an image that would add meaning to a section of their own writing that goes beyond simply illustrating what the words already say.
exampleOfSuccess: Student writes a sentence about a character feeling nervous and then describes: 'I would draw her biting her nails and looking at the clock — the words don't say she was checking the time but it would show she was waiting for something.'
commonError: Student describes an image that simply restates the written content rather than adding new meaning.

name: Replaces an everyday word with topic-specific vocabulary
description: Student can identify an everyday or vague word in a piece of writing and replace it with a more precise or topic-specific word that better suits the context.
exampleOfSuccess: Student reads 'The animal moved quickly through the water.' and replaces 'moved' with 'darted' and 'animal' with 'dolphin' to better suit a text about ocean creatures.
commonError: Student replaces a word with a synonym of similar vagueness rather than selecting more precise vocabulary.

name: Identifies and explains new vocabulary from a text
description: Student can identify words they were unfamiliar with in a learning area text
sequenceOrder: use context clues to infer meaning
difficultyStage: and explain the word in their own terms.
commonError: early
checkpointTask: After reading a science text, student identifies 'carnivore' as a new word, uses the surrounding sentences to infer it means 'an animal that eats meat', and correctly uses it in a new sentence.
isOptional: Student copies the dictionary definition without explaining meaning in their own words, or cannot use context to infer meaning without direct instruction.

name: Selects vocabulary to match a character or setting
description: Student can choose vocabulary that is appropriate to the type of character or setting they are writing about
sequenceOrder: drawing on words that convey mood
commonError: middle
checkpointTask: When writing about a wizard character, student uses 'muttered', 'ancient', 'shadowy' and 'enchanted' rather than 'said', 'old', 'dark' and 'magic', explaining the first set sounds more like a fantasy story.
isOptional: Student uses vocabulary from the model text without demonstrating awareness of why those words were chosen or what effect they create.

name: Makes deliberate vocabulary choices in own writing
description: Student can explain at least one vocabulary choice in their own writing
sequenceOrder: articulating why a particular word was selected over an alternative.
exampleOfSuccess: late
commonError: During a writing conference, student explains: 'I used 'crept' instead of 'walked' because I wanted it to sound like he was trying not to be noticed — 'walked' is too ordinary for that.'
checkpointTask: Student makes interesting vocabulary choices but cannot articulate the reasoning behind them when asked.

name: Identifies capital letters in titles
description: Student can locate capital letters used in titles of texts (books
sequenceOrder: films
exampleOfSuccess: songs) and explain why they are used there.
isOptional: Student finds three book titles in the classroom and identifies the capital letters, explaining: 'Every important word in a title has a capital letter so you know it's a title.'
isArchived: Student identifies the capital letters but explains them as the start of a sentence rather than as a feature of titles.

name: Uses capital letters correctly in titles when writing
description: Student can write a title for their own text using capital letters correctly on important words.
exampleOfSuccess: Student writes the title 'The Adventures of a Tiny Snail' with capital letters on 'The', 'Adventures', 'Tiny' and 'Snail' but not on 'of' and 'a'.
commonError: Student either capitalises every word in the title (including articles and prepositions) or only the first word.

name: Identifies commas used in a list
description: Student can locate commas used to separate items in a list within a sentence and explain that commas replace the word 'and' between items.
exampleOfSuccess: In the sentence 'The bag contained a pencil, a ruler, some sticky tape and a notebook.' student identifies the commas and explains they separate the items in the list.
commonError: Student identifies commas in the text but cannot explain their function, or confuses list commas with other punctuation.

name: Uses commas in a list in own writing
description: Student can write a sentence containing a list of three or more items
sequenceOrder: using commas to separate them correctly.
exampleOfSuccess: middle
commonError: Student writes: 'For the party we need balloons, streamers, party hats and a cake.' using commas between all items except before the final 'and'.
checkpointTask: Student either omits all commas in a list or places a comma before 'and' at the end of the list (Oxford comma — not standard in Australian English).

name: Edits writing for correct use of capitals in titles and commas in lists
description: Student can read back their own or a peer's writing and identify and correct errors in the use of capital letters in titles and commas in lists.
exampleOfSuccess: Student reviews a draft that contains 'the three Little pigs' and 'We need paper glue and scissors.' and corrects both: 'The Three Little Pigs' and 'We need paper, glue and scissors.'
commonError: Student identifies one type of error but misses the other, or corrects surface features without understanding the underlying rule.
